source.text: וְעַתָּ֤ה׀שָֽׂחֲק֣וּ עָלַי֮ צְעִירִ֥ים מִמֶּ֗נִּי לְיָ֫מִ֥ים אֲשֶׁר־מָאַ֥סְתִּי אֲבוֹתָ֑ם לָ֝שִׁ֗ית עִם־כַּלְבֵ֥י צֹאנִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: And now they laugh at me, [those] younger than I in days, whose fathers I rejected to put with [the] dogs of my flock.

en.L: And now they laugh at me, \q [those] younger than I in days, \q whose fathers I refused to put \q with the dogs of my flock.
en.B: But now they laugh at me, \q men younger than I am, \q whose fathers I would have refused \q to put with my sheepdogs.
en.R: But now younger men laugh at me. \q I would not even have trusted their fathers \q to help my dogs guard my sheep.

decisions.choice: And now: the present set against the past of chapter 29
decisions.reason: "And now" marks the turn from Job's memories to his present misery, and comes again at the start of verses 9 and 16.

decisions.choice: not fit to put with the dogs of my flock: utterly worthless in Job's eyes
decisions.reason: Sheepdogs were among the lowliest helpers on a farm. Job would not have trusted the fathers of these men even with the dogs' work. The words are harsh: they show how far below Job these men once stood, and so how deep his fall is.

decisions.choice: younger: in a culture that honored age, mockery from the young was shameful
decisions.reason: The young were expected to show respect to their elders, as they did to Job in 29:8. Now young men of no standing mock him (19:18).

decisions.choice: But now
decisions.reason: The "and" introduces a contrast (m1).

decisions.choice: men
decisions.reason: The mockers are particular young men, the sons of an outcast group (verses 1-8).

source.text: גַּם־כֹּ֣חַ יְ֭דֵיהֶם לָ֣מָּה לִּ֑י עָ֝לֵ֗ימוֹ אָ֣בַד כָּֽלַח׃

records.literal_gloss: Also [the] strength of their hands, why [is it] to me? On them has perished vigor.

en.L: Also the strength of their hands, what [use was it] to me? \q Vigor had perished from them.
en.B: What use to me was the strength of their hands, \q men whose vigor was gone?
en.R: Their strength was no use to me. \q They were too weak to work.

decisions.choice: vigor: the full strength of mature life
decisions.reason: The word (kelach) is rare; in 5:26 it names the ripe age at which a person goes to the grave in full strength. Here it means the fathers were worn out, past useful work.

decisions.choice: the fathers' strength was of no use to Job
decisions.reason: "Their hands" most naturally refers to the fathers of verse 1, men too broken to be worth hiring. Verses 3-8 describe their whole outcast class.

decisions.choice: the two lines joined into one question (B) or two statements (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced joins the line about vigor to the question as a description of the men; Readable states the point of the rhetorical question plainly.

source.text: בְּחֶ֥סֶר וּבְכָפָ֗ן גַּ֫לְמ֥וּד הַֽעֹרְקִ֥ים צִיָּ֑ה אֶ֝֗מֶשׁ שׁוֹאָ֥ה וּמְשֹׁאָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: In want and in hunger, gaunt, those who gnaw [the] dry land, [in the] darkness of devastation and desolation,

en.L: In want and in hunger [they were] gaunt, \q those who gnaw the dry land, \q [in the] gloom of waste and desolation;
en.B: Gaunt with want and hunger, \q they gnawed the dry ground, \q in the gloom of waste and desolation.
en.R: They were thin from poverty and hunger. \q They chewed whatever they could find in the dry desert, \q in dark and empty places.

decisions.choice: gaunt: hard and barren, worn thin
decisions.reason: The word (galmud) is used of a barren woman (3:7; Isaiah 49:21) and of hard, stony things; here of people wasted by hunger.

decisions.choice: gnaw the dry land: chew whatever the desert gives
decisions.reason: The verb ('araq) is rare; it is used again in verse 17 of gnawing pain, and in Aramaic means "to flee". The likelier sense is that they chewed the dry roots and plants of the desert (verse 4). If it means "flee", they fled into the desert; both show their misery.

decisions.choice: darkness: gloom or night
decisions.reason: The word ('emesh) elsewhere means "last night" or "yesterday" (Genesis 31:29). Here it seems to mean the gloom of a waste place, or that they spent the night there.

decisions.choice: waste and desolation: a wordplay, utter wasteland
decisions.reason: The two words (sho'ah, mesho'ah) come from the same root and sound alike, as in 38:27 and Zephaniah 1:15. The pair stresses how barren the place is.

source.text: הַקֹּטְפִ֣ים מַלּ֣וּחַ עֲלֵי־שִׂ֑יחַ וְשֹׁ֖רֶשׁ רְתָמִ֣ים לַחְמָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Those who pluck saltwort by [the] bush, and [the] root of broom [is] their food.

en.L: who pluck saltwort among [the] bushes, \q and the root of [the] broom [is] their food.
en.B: They pick salt plants among the bushes, \q and the roots of the broom tree are their food.
en.R: They pick bitter plants from the bushes \q and eat the roots of desert shrubs.

decisions.choice: saltwort: a salty desert plant eaten only in famine
decisions.reason: The word (malluach) comes from the word for salt; it names a sour, salty plant of dry country, food only for the starving.

decisions.choice: the root of the broom tree as food
decisions.reason: The broom (rotem) is a desert bush (1 Kings 19:4) whose roots are bitter and were burned for charcoal (Psalm 120:4). Hebrew "their bread" (lachmam) is most simply "their food", food of last resort. A slight change in the letters would give "to warm themselves", burning the roots for heat.

decisions.choice: bitter plants; desert shrubs
decisions.reason: Readable describes the plants instead of naming them.

source.text: מִן־גֵּ֥ו יְגֹרָ֑שׁוּ יָרִ֥יעוּ עָ֝לֵ֗ימוֹ כַּגַּנָּֽב׃

records.literal_gloss: From [the] community they are driven out; people shout at them as [at] a thief.

en.L: From [the] community they are driven out; \q [people] shout at them as [at] a thief.
en.B: They are driven out from human company; \q people shout after them as after a thief.
en.R: They are chased away from towns, \q and people shout at them as if they were thieves.

decisions.choice: the community: the midst of people, settled society
decisions.reason: The word (gev) means the middle or inside; here, the inside of the community, from which they are expelled.

decisions.choice: shout at them as at a thief: the hue and cry raised to drive off a thief
decisions.reason: When a thief was seen, people shouted and chased him off. These outcasts were driven off the same way whenever they came near.

decisions.choice: people
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject; English supplies one.

source.text: בַּעֲר֣וּץ נְחָלִ֣ים לִשְׁכֹּ֑ן חֹרֵ֖י עָפָ֣ר וְכֵפִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: In [the] slope of [the] wadis [they have] to dwell, [in] holes of [the] ground and [in] rocks.

en.L: In the gullies of [the] wadis [they have] to dwell, \q [in] holes of [the] ground and [in] the rocks.
en.B: They have to live on the slopes of the dry ravines, \q in holes in the ground and among the rocks.
en.R: They have to live in dry riverbeds, \q in holes in the ground and among the rocks.

decisions.choice: the slopes of the wadis: steep sides of dry stream beds
decisions.reason: A wadi (nachal) is a valley that fills with water only in the rainy season (6:15). Its steep, rough sides are a place no one would choose to live.

decisions.choice: to dwell: they are forced to live there
decisions.reason: The infinitive "to dwell" says what is left to them: such places are all they have.

source.text: בֵּין־שִׂיחִ֥ים יִנְהָ֑קוּ תַּ֖חַת חָר֣וּל יְסֻפָּֽחוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Among [the] bushes they bray; under [the] nettles they huddle together.

en.L: Among [the] bushes they bray; \q under [the] nettles they huddle together.
en.B: They bray among the bushes \q and huddle together under the nettles.
en.R: They howl like wild donkeys among the bushes \q and crowd together under the weeds.

decisions.choice: they bray: they cry out like wild donkeys
decisions.reason: The verb is used of the wild donkey crying for food (6:5). Job pictures the outcasts as hungry animals in the desert, as in 24:5.

decisions.choice: nettles: thorny weeds
decisions.reason: The word (charul) names a prickly weed of waste ground (Proverbs 24:31; Zephaniah 2:9).

decisions.choice: howl like wild donkeys
decisions.reason: Readable says what the verb pictures (m1).

source.text: בְּֽנֵי־נָ֭בָל גַּם־בְּנֵ֣י בְלִי־שֵׁ֑ם נִ֝כְּא֗וּ מִן־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

records.literal_gloss: Sons of a fool, also sons of no name, they have been whipped out of the land.

en.L: Sons of a fool, also sons of no name, \q they have been whipped out of the land.
en.B: A senseless and nameless brood, \q they were driven out of the land with whips.
en.R: They are worthless people with no family name, \q driven out of the country with whips.

decisions.choice: sons of a fool, sons of no name: worthless people with no honored family
decisions.reason: "Son of" describes what a person belongs to. A fool (naval) is a godless, worthless person (2:10; 1 Samuel 25:25). "No name" means no reputation and no family standing; a good name was a person's honor.

decisions.choice: whipped out: driven out by blows
decisions.reason: The verb (naka') means to strike or beat; they were beaten out of the settled land.

decisions.choice: a brood (B); people (R)
decisions.reason: The phrase means a class of people, not literal sons (m1); Literal keeps "sons".

source.text: וְ֭עַתָּה נְגִינָתָ֣ם הָיִ֑יתִי וָאֱהִ֖י לָהֶ֣ם לְמִלָּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And now their song I have become, and I have become to them a byword.

en.L: And now I have become their song, \q and I have become a byword to them.
en.B: And now I have become their mocking song; \q I have become a byword among them.
en.R: And now these people make up songs to mock me. \q They use my name as a joke.

decisions.choice: their song: a mocking song about Job
decisions.reason: The word (neginah) is a song played on strings; here, as in Lamentations 3:14, 63, a taunt song in which the sufferer is mocked.

decisions.choice: a byword: a word people use to mock
decisions.reason: The word (millah) usually means a word; here it means that Job has become a saying, a name used in scorn (17:6).

decisions.choice: use my name as a joke
decisions.reason: Readable explains "byword", which many readers do not know.

source.text: תִּֽ֭עֲבוּנִי רָ֣חֲקוּ מֶ֑נִּי וּ֝מִפָּנַ֗י לֹא־חָ֥שְׂכוּ רֹֽק׃

records.literal_gloss: They abhor me, they keep far from me, and from my face they do not withhold spit.

en.L: They abhor me; they keep far from me, \q and from my face they do not hold back spit.
en.B: They detest me and keep their distance from me; \q they do not hesitate to spit in my face.
en.R: They hate me and stay away from me. \q They even spit in my face.

decisions.choice: spit from my face: spitting at him, the worst public insult
alternatives: spitting at the sight of him
decisions.reason: Spitting in someone's face was a deep public disgrace (17:6; Numbers 12:14; Deuteronomy 25:9; Isaiah 50:6). The Hebrew "from my face" may mean in his face or at the sight of him; either way it is open contempt.

decisions.choice: do not hesitate (B); even (R)
decisions.reason: The negative "they do not withhold" means they spit freely; Balanced and Readable say so positively.

source.text: כִּֽי־יִתְרִ֣י פִ֭תַּח וַיְעַנֵּ֑נִי וְ֝רֶ֗סֶן מִפָּנַ֥י שִׁלֵּֽחוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: For my cord he has loosened and afflicted me, and the bridle before me they have thrown off.

en.L: Because {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has loosened my cord and afflicted me, \q they have thrown off the bridle before me.
en.B: Because God has loosened my bowstring and humbled me, \q they have thrown off all restraint in my presence.
en.R: God has taken away my strength and brought me down, \q so they act without any restraint toward me.

decisions.choice: my cord: the reading of the margin (qere)
decisions.reason: The written text has "his cord" (yitro); the margin tells the reader to read "my cord" (yitri), which the text here gives and which fits the first person through the verse. With the written form it would mean the mocker has let loose his own cord, throwing off restraint, which the second line says anyway.

decisions.choice: loosened my cord: took away Job's strength and standing
alternatives: untied the cord of my tent
decisions.reason: The cord (yeter) can be a bowstring or a tent cord. A loosened bowstring is strength taken away, the opposite of the renewed bow of 29:20; a loosened tent cord is a life collapsing (4:21). Either picture means that God has made Job powerless.

decisions.choice: he: God
decisions.reason: The subject is not named. Job's complaints elsewhere name God as the one who has brought him low (19:6-13), and verses 19-23 address God; the change from "he" to "they" also points to God as the one who acts first.

decisions.choice: threw off the bridle: dropped all restraint
decisions.reason: A bridle holds an animal in check. Before Job they no longer hold anything back.

decisions.choice: God
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the subject as God (m3); Literal keeps "he" with a deity_pronoun span.

source.text: עַל־יָמִין֮ פִּרְחַ֪ח יָ֫ק֥וּמוּ רַגְלַ֥י שִׁלֵּ֑חוּ וַיָּסֹ֥לּוּ עָ֝לַ֗י אָרְח֥וֹת אֵידָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: On [the] right a brood rises; my feet they push away, and they cast up against me [the] paths of their ruin.

en.L: On [my] right [the] brood rises; \q they push away my feet, \q and they build up against me their ways of ruin.
en.B: On my right the rabble rises up; \q they trip up my feet \q and build their siege ramps of ruin against me.
en.R: This mob attacks me from my right side. \q They knock my feet out from under me. \q They attack me as an army attacks a city.

decisions.choice: a brood: a mob of young people
decisions.reason: The word (pirchach) is found only here; it comes from a verb meaning to sprout, and seems to mean a young brood or rabble, the young men of verse 1.

decisions.choice: on the right: the side of a defender or accuser in court
decisions.reason: The right side was where an accuser or a defender stood (Psalm 109:6, 31; Zechariah 3:1). The mob stands where an accuser would.

decisions.choice: cast up ways of ruin: build siege ramps against him
decisions.reason: The verb (salal) is used of throwing up earth for a siege ramp (19:12; 2 Samuel 20:15). Job pictures himself as a city besieged by the mob, as he pictured God's troops besieging him in 19:12.

decisions.choice: build siege ramps (B); attack ... as an army attacks a city (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced names the picture of the siege (m3); Readable explains it.

source.text: נָתְס֗וּ נְֽתִיבָ֫תִ֥י לְהַוָּתִ֥י יֹעִ֑ילוּ לֹ֖א עֹזֵ֣ר לָֽמוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: They break up my path; to my destruction they profit; [there is] no helper to them.

en.L: They tear up my path; \q they profit from my destruction; \q [there is] no helper for them.
en.B: They break up my path; \q they help my destruction along, \q and no one holds them back.
en.R: They block every way I could escape. \q They work hard to destroy me, \q and no one stops them.

decisions.choice: profit from my destruction: push on Job's ruin
decisions.reason: The verb (ya'al) means to profit or be useful. Here it most likely means they help his ruin along.

decisions.choice: no helper to them: no one restrains them
alternatives: they need no one to help them
no one helps me against them
decisions.reason: The last line is short and unclear. It may mean that no one stands in their way, or that they need no help to do it. Either way Job is defenseless.

source.text: כְּפֶ֣רֶץ רָחָ֣ב יֶאֱתָ֑יוּ תַּ֥חַת שֹׁ֝אָ֗ה הִתְגַּלְגָּֽלוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Like [through] a wide breach they come; under [the] crash they roll themselves on.

en.L: As [through] a wide breach they come; \q amid [the] crash they roll on.
en.B: They come in as through a wide breach in the wall; \q amid the crash of ruins they roll on.
en.R: They pour in as if the city wall had broken open. \q They rush at me as the wall comes crashing down.

decisions.choice: a wide breach and a crash: the siege ends with the wall broken
decisions.reason: The siege picture of verse 12 goes on: the wall is breached (16:14) and the attackers pour in among the falling stones.

decisions.choice: the crash: the noise of ruin
decisions.reason: The word (sho'ah) means devastation and the roar of ruin (30:3; Proverbs 1:27).

decisions.choice: in the wall (B); the city wall (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the siege picture clear (m1).

source.text: הָהְפַּ֥ךְ עָלַ֗י בַּלָּ֫ה֥וֹת תִּרְדֹּ֣ף כָּ֭רוּחַ נְדִבָתִ֑י וּ֝כְעָ֗ב עָבְרָ֥ה יְשֻׁעָתִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: Turned upon me [are] terrors; it pursues like the wind my dignity, and like a cloud has passed away my safety.

en.L: Terrors are turned upon me; \q my dignity is chased away as by the wind, \q and like a cloud my safety has passed away.
en.B: Terrors are turned against me; \q my honor is driven away as by the wind, \q and my safety has vanished like a cloud.
en.R: Terrors attack me. \q My good name is blown away like the wind, \q and my safety is gone like a cloud.

decisions.choice: terrors: sudden, overwhelming dread
decisions.reason: The word (ballahah) names the terrors of disaster and death (18:11, 14; 27:20).

decisions.choice: my dignity ... my safety: Job's standing and security
decisions.reason: The first word (nedivah) means nobility or honor (as in a noble, 12:21). The second (yeshu'ah) usually means rescue or salvation; here it means the security and well-being Job once had.

decisions.choice: it pursues: the terror drives away Job's honor
decisions.reason: The verb is feminine singular or second person; it most likely takes the terror as its subject. Some read "you pursue", addressed to God. The sense is that Job's honor is gone like a wind.

decisions.choice: my dignity is chased away (L); my honor is driven away (B)
alternatives: it pursues my dignity like the wind
decisions.reason: English gives the line a passive form to keep the picture clear (m3).

source.text: וְעַתָּ֗ה עָ֭לַי תִּשְׁתַּפֵּ֣ךְ נַפְשִׁ֑י יֹ֭אחֲז֣וּנִי יְמֵי־עֹֽנִי׃

records.literal_gloss: And now upon me pours itself out my soul; seize me days of affliction.

en.L: And now my soul pours itself out within me; \q days of affliction have seized me.
en.B: And now my life is poured out within me; \q days of suffering have taken hold of me.
en.R: And now I am close to dying. \q Day after day I suffer.

decisions.choice: my soul pours itself out: my life is ebbing away
decisions.reason: The soul (nefesh) is a person's life; to pour it out is to lose strength and come near death (Psalm 42:5; Lamentations 2:12; Isaiah 53:12). "Upon me" is Hebrew for "within me".

decisions.choice: And now: the third turn to the present
decisions.reason: After verses 1 and 9, Job turns a third time to his present state, now his body and his pain (verses 16-19).

decisions.choice: my life
decisions.reason: In English "soul" suggests the immortal part of a person; the Hebrew means his life (m1). Literal keeps "soul".

decisions.choice: I am close to dying
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the picture means (m1).

source.text: לַ֗יְלָה עֲ֭צָמַי נִקַּ֣ר מֵעָלָ֑י וְ֝עֹרְקַ֗י לֹ֣א יִשְׁכָּבֽוּן׃

records.literal_gloss: [By] night my bones it pierces from upon me, and my gnawing [pains] do not lie down.

en.L: [By] night it pierces my bones [and takes them] from me, \q and my gnawing [pains] do not rest.
en.B: At night my bones are pierced within me, \q and the pains that gnaw at me never rest.
en.R: At night my bones ache as if something were stabbing them, \q and the pain never stops.

decisions.choice: it pierces: the night, or the illness, pierces his bones
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject other than "night", which may be the subject (the night pierces) or the time (at night it pierces). Either way the pain is worst at night (7:3-4).

decisions.choice: my gnawing pains: pains that eat at him
decisions.reason: The word comes from the verb "gnaw" of verse 3. It most likely names gnawing pains; some take it as "my sinews" or as gnawing creatures (7:5).

decisions.choice: do not lie down: never rest
decisions.reason: The pains, like a restless watcher, never lie down to sleep.

decisions.choice: my bones are pierced
decisions.reason: Balanced uses a passive, leaving the unnamed subject open as the Hebrew does (m1).

source.text: בְּרָב־כֹּ֭חַיִתְחַפֵּ֣שׂ לְבוּשִׁ֑י כְּפִ֖י כֻתָּנְתִּ֣י יַֽאַזְרֵֽנִי׃

records.literal_gloss: By great force my garment is disfigured; like [the] mouth of my tunic it binds me.

en.L: By great force my garment is disfigured; \q like [the] collar of my tunic it binds me.
en.B: With great force my clothing is twisted out of shape; \q it binds me like the collar of my tunic.
en.R: My illness has twisted my body like a garment pulled out of shape. \q It grips me tight, like a shirt collar around my neck.

decisions.choice: my garment is disfigured: Job's body, wasted by illness, like a garment pulled out of shape
decisions.reason: The verb (chafas, in this form) means to disguise oneself or be changed in appearance (1 Kings 22:30). The line most likely says Job's illness has so changed him that his clothing hangs wrongly on him, or that his skin, his "garment" (10:11), is disfigured. The Greek translation reads "seizes", with God as the one who grabs his clothes. The Hebrew is uncertain.

decisions.choice: the mouth of my tunic: the neck opening of the inner garment
decisions.reason: The tunic (kuttonet) was the long shirt worn next to the body; its "mouth" is the opening for the head (Exodus 28:32; Psalm 133:2). Something gripping like a tight collar is a picture of being choked or held fast.

decisions.choice: it binds me: the illness, or God, holds him fast
decisions.reason: The verb can be read "it" or "he". It may be the illness or God; verse 19 goes on with "he has thrown me", and verses 20-23 speak to God.

decisions.choice: My illness has twisted my body
decisions.reason: Readable follows the likelier reading (m1) and names the illness as the cause; the cause is not named in the Hebrew.

source.text: הֹרָ֥נִי לַחֹ֑מֶר וָ֝אֶתְמַשֵּׁ֗ל כֶּעָפָ֥ר וָאֵֽפֶר׃

records.literal_gloss: He has thrown me into [the] mud, and I have become like dust and ashes.

en.L: He has thrown me into the mud, \q and I have become like dust and ashes.
en.B: He has thrown me into the mud, \q and I have become like dust and ashes.
en.R: God has thrown me into the mud. \q I am no better than dust and ashes.

decisions.choice: He: God
decisions.reason: The subject is not named, but Job means God, whom he addresses from verse 20 on.

decisions.choice: dust and ashes: worthless, brought to nothing
decisions.reason: Abraham called himself "dust and ashes" before God (Genesis 18:27). Job sits among the ashes (2:8), and will use the same words at the end (42:6).

decisions.choice: God
decisions.reason: Readable names the subject (m1).

source.text: אֲשַׁוַּ֣ע אֵ֭לֶיךָ וְלֹ֣א תַעֲנֵ֑נִי עָ֝מַ֗דְתִּי וַתִּתְבֹּ֥נֶן בִּֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: I cry for help to you, and you do not answer me; I stand, and you look at me.

en.L: I cry to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} for help, and {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} do not answer me; \q I stand, and {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} [only] look at me.
en.B: I cry to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} for help, but {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} do not answer me; \q I stand up, and {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} merely look at me.
en.R: I cry out to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} for help, but {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} do not answer. \q I stand before {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, and {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} just stare at me.

decisions.choice: you: Job now speaks to God directly
decisions.reason: From here to verse 23 Job turns from describing his state to speaking to God, as he did in chapters 7, 10 and 13-14.

decisions.choice: you look at me: God only looks, without helping
alternatives: you do not look at me
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "you look at me". Some old manuscripts and translations carry the "not" of the first line over, "you do not look at me". As it stands, God's look is cold: he watches and does nothing, as Job complained in 7:19-20.

decisions.choice: [only] (L); merely (B); just stare (R)
decisions.reason: The contrast with the cry for help shows that looking is all God does (m2); each level marks it.

source.text: תֵּהָפֵ֣ךְ לְאַכְזָ֣ר לִ֑י בְּעֹ֖צֶם יָדְךָ֣ תִשְׂטְמֵֽנִי׃

records.literal_gloss: You have turned into one cruel to me; with [the] might of your hand you are hostile to me.

en.L: You have turned cruel to me; \q with the might of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} hand {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} persecute me.
en.B: You have turned cruel toward me; \q with the strength of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} hand {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} attack me.
en.R: You have become cruel to me. \q You use all {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} power to attack me.

decisions.choice: you have turned: God has changed toward Job
decisions.reason: The verb (hafakh) means to turn or be changed. Job feels that the God who once watched over him (29:2) has turned into his enemy (13:24; 16:9; 19:11).

decisions.choice: you are hostile to me: you hold a grudge against me and attack me
decisions.reason: The verb (satam) means to bear a grudge and act on it (16:9; Genesis 27:41; 50:15). It is close in sound and sense to the verb behind the Accuser's title (1:6), though it is a different word.

source.text: תִּשָּׂאֵ֣נִי אֶל־ר֭וּחַתַּרְכִּיבֵ֑נִי וּ֝תְמֹגְגֵ֗נִי תּוּשִׁיָּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: You lift me up to [the] wind; you make me ride; and you dissolve me [in the] storm.

en.L: You lift me up on the wind [and] make me ride [it], \q and {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} toss me about [in the] roar [of the storm].
en.B: You lift me up on the wind and make me ride it; \q {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} toss me about in the roar of the storm.
en.R: You pick me up and let the wind carry me away. \q You throw me around in the storm.

decisions.choice: lift me on the wind, make me ride: Job is helpless, carried off like chaff
decisions.reason: Job is like straw or chaff caught up by the wind (13:25; 21:18), with no say in where he goes.

decisions.choice: toss me in the roar of the storm: the written text
alternatives: the reading of the margin, "you melt away success" or "you melt me away; [there is no] sound wisdom"
decisions.reason: The written text has a word (teshuwah) meaning a crash or roar, as of a storm (36:29). The margin (qere), which the text here prints, has a similar word (tushiyyah) meaning success or sound wisdom (5:12; 6:13), which is hard to fit into the line. The written form fits the picture of the wind. The verb (mug) means to melt away or be shaken apart.

decisions.choice: toss me about
decisions.reason: The verb pictures being shaken apart; in a storm, "toss about" says this in English.

source.text: כִּֽי־יָ֭דַעְתִּי מָ֣וֶת תְּשִׁיבֵ֑נִי וּבֵ֖ית מוֹעֵ֣ד לְכָל־חָֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: For I know [to] death you will bring me back, and [to the] house of meeting for every living [one].

en.L: For I know [that] {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will bring me back [to] death, \q and [to the] house appointed for all [the] living.
en.B: For I know that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will bring me to death, \q to the house appointed for all the living.
en.R: I know {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will bring me to my death, \q to the place where everyone who lives must go.

decisions.choice: bring me back to death: return me to the dust
decisions.reason: The verb (shuv) means to bring back. It recalls that people return to the dust they came from (10:9; Genesis 3:19; Ecclesiastes 12:7).

decisions.choice: the house of meeting: the grave, where all the living are brought together
decisions.reason: The word (mo'ed) means an appointed meeting place or time. The grave is the place appointed for everyone (3:17-19; 17:13; Ecclesiastes 12:5).

decisions.choice: bring me to death
decisions.reason: "Back to death" would puzzle an English reader; the sense of return is explained in m1.

source.text: אַ֣ךְ לֹא־בְ֭עִי יִשְׁלַח־יָ֑ד אִם־בְּ֝פִיד֗וֹ לָהֶ֥ן שֽׁוּעַ׃

records.literal_gloss: Surely not against a heap of ruins does one stretch out a hand, if in his disaster [there is] to them a cry for help?

en.L: Surely one does not stretch out a hand against a ruin, \q if in his disaster [there is] for them a cry for help?
en.B: Yet does not someone in ruins stretch out a hand, \q and cry for help in his disaster?
en.R: But surely a person who is ruined reaches out a hand \q and calls for help when disaster comes.

decisions.choice: a ruined person reaches out for help: Job's cry is natural
alternatives: no one strikes a ruined man
God does not reach out against a ruin, so why against me
one does not reach out to a heap of ruins (it is useless)
decisions.reason: This is one of the hardest lines in the chapter. The words are "surely not on a heap of ruins does one send out a hand, if in his disaster to them a cry for help". Read as a question, it means that anyone who is ruined will stretch out a hand and cry for help, as Job is doing (verse 20). Other readings: no one strikes a person already in ruins, which God is doing to Job; or the hand stretched out is someone else's, a helper's. The next verse speaks of Job helping others, which suits the reading about reaching out for help.

decisions.choice: a heap of ruins: a ruined person
decisions.reason: The word ('i) means a heap of rubble, as of a destroyed city (Micah 3:12). Here it most likely pictures a person in ruins.

decisions.choice: Yet does not ... ? (B); But surely ... (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable follow the reading in m1; Literal keeps the Hebrew words as near as English allows.

source.text: אִם־לֹ֣א בָ֭כִיתִי לִקְשֵׁה־י֑וֹם עָֽגְמָ֥ה נַ֝פְשִׁ֗י לָאֶבְיֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: Did I not weep for [the one] hard of day? Was my soul not grieved for the needy?

en.L: Did I not weep for [the one whose] day [was] hard? \q Was my soul not grieved for the needy?
en.B: Did I not weep for those in trouble? \q Did I not grieve for the needy?
en.R: I cried for people who were having hard times. \q I was sad for poor people.

decisions.choice: hard of day: one who has hard times
decisions.reason: "Hard of day" means someone whose days are hard, someone in trouble (compare 1 Samuel 1:15, "hard of spirit").

decisions.choice: Did I not ...? : questions expecting "yes"
decisions.reason: Both lines are questions that mean "I did". Job contrasts the pity he showed (29:12-16) with the pity no one, God included, shows him (verse 26).

decisions.choice: statements in place of questions
decisions.reason: Readable states the answer the questions expect (m2).

source.text: כִּ֤י ט֣וֹב קִ֭וִּיתִי וַיָּ֣בֹא רָ֑ע וַֽאֲיַחֲלָ֥ה לְ֝א֗וֹר וַיָּ֥בֹא אֹֽפֶל׃

records.literal_gloss: For good I hoped for, and came evil; and I waited for light, and came darkness.

en.L: For I hoped for good, and evil came; \q and I waited for light, and darkness came.
en.B: Yet when I hoped for good, evil came; \q when I waited for light, darkness came.
en.R: But when I hoped for good things, bad things came. \q When I looked for light, darkness came.

decisions.choice: For: the reason for the cry of verse 24 or the contrast with verse 25
decisions.reason: The word ki ties the verse to what came before: Job, who wept for others (verse 25), has met evil instead of the good he could expect.

decisions.choice: light and darkness: well-being and disaster
decisions.reason: Light pictures life and good days, darkness trouble and death, as in 29:3 and chapter 3.

decisions.choice: Yet when (B); But when (R)
decisions.reason: The verse states a contrast with what Job had a right to expect (m1); Balanced and Readable mark it.

source.text: מֵעַ֖י רֻתְּח֥וּ וְלֹא־דָ֗מּוּ קִדְּמֻ֥נִי יְמֵי־עֹֽנִי׃

records.literal_gloss: My inward parts are made to boil, and they are not still; days of affliction confront me.

en.L: My inward parts boil and are not still; \q days of affliction confront me.
en.B: My insides churn and are never still; \q days of suffering confront me.
en.R: I am always upset inside. \q Day after day I meet more suffering.

decisions.choice: my inward parts boil: deep inner distress
decisions.reason: The inward parts (me'im), the bowels, were felt as the seat of deep feeling (Lamentations 1:20; Isaiah 16:11). Boiling pictures turmoil that will not settle.

decisions.choice: one colon: the accents give the verse no main division
decisions.reason: The accents give this verse no main division, only a lesser pause before "days of affliction"; the line is broken there.

source.text: קֹדֵ֣ר הִ֭לַּכְתִּי בְּלֹ֣א חַמָּ֑ה קַ֖מְתִּי בַקָּהָ֣ל אֲשַׁוֵּֽעַ׃

records.literal_gloss: Dark I go about, without sun; I stand in the assembly, I cry for help.

en.L: Darkened I go about, without [the] sun; \q I stand up in the assembly [and] cry for help.
en.B: I go about blackened, but not by the sun; \q I stand up in the assembly and cry for help.
en.R: I walk around with darkened skin, but not from the sun. \q I stand up in public and cry for help.

decisions.choice: dark, without sun: blackened by illness, not by the sun; or mourning, without warmth
alternatives: going about in mourning, without the sun's warmth
decisions.reason: The word (qoder) means dark or dirty and is used of mourners going about in dark clothes and unwashed (5:11; Psalm 38:7). "Without sun" (chammah, the sun's heat) seems to say that the darkness of his skin is not sunburn (verse 30). It may also mean he mourns in a sunless gloom.

decisions.choice: the assembly: the gathering of the community
decisions.reason: The word (qahal) means a gathering of people; Job cries out in public, where he once sat in honor (29:7).

decisions.choice: but not by the sun
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable follow the first reading in m1.

source.text: אָ֭ח הָיִ֣יתִי לְתַנִּ֑ים וְ֝רֵ֗עַ לִבְנ֥וֹת יַעֲנָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: A brother I have become to jackals, and a companion to daughters of [the] ostrich.

en.L: I have become a brother to jackals \q and a companion to ostriches.
en.B: I have become a brother to jackals \q and a companion to ostriches.
en.R: I howl like the jackals \q and cry like the ostriches.

decisions.choice: brother to jackals, companion to ostriches: living in the waste, crying mournfully
decisions.reason: Jackals and ostriches live in desolate places and are known for their wailing cries (Micah 1:8; Isaiah 34:13; 43:20). Job is cut off from people and cries like them.

decisions.choice: daughters of the ostrich: ostriches
decisions.reason: "Daughters of" with an animal names the creatures themselves. The bird (ya'anah) is most likely the ostrich (Lamentations 4:3); some think it is an owl.

decisions.choice: I howl like ... cry like
alternatives: I have become a brother to ... a companion to
decisions.reason: Readable says what the picture means (m1).

source.text: ע֭וֹרִישָׁחַ֣ר מֵעָלָ֑י וְעַצְמִי־חָ֝֗רָה מִנִּי־חֹֽרֶב׃

records.literal_gloss: My skin has become black [and falls] from upon me, and my bone burns from heat.

en.L: My skin has turned black [and falls] from me, \q and my bones burn with heat.
en.B: My skin turns black and peels from me, \q and my bones burn with fever.
en.R: My skin has turned black and is peeling off, \q and my body burns with fever.

decisions.choice: skin turned black: the effect of Job's illness
decisions.reason: Job's disease (2:7) darkens and peels his skin (7:5).

decisions.choice: heat: fever
decisions.reason: The word (chorev) means heat or dryness; burning bones mean a fever inside his body (Psalm 102:4).

decisions.choice: [and falls] (L); and peels (B); and is peeling off (R)
decisions.reason: "From upon me" implies the skin coming away; English needs a verb.

source.text: וַיְהִ֣י לְ֭אֵבֶל כִּנֹּרִ֑י וְ֝עֻגָבִ֗י לְק֣וֹל בֹּכִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And has become [for] mourning my lyre, and my flute [for the] sound of those who weep.

en.L: And my lyre has become [for] mourning, \q and my flute [for the] sound of those who weep.
en.B: My lyre is tuned to mourning, \q and my flute to the sound of weeping.
en.R: My music has turned into sad songs; \q the only sound I make is weeping.

decisions.choice: lyre and flute: the instruments of celebration
decisions.reason: The lyre (kinnor) and the flute ('ugav) were played at feasts and in joy (21:12; Genesis 4:21). Now they play laments. The chapter ends in mourning, as chapter 29 ended with Job comforting mourners.

decisions.choice: My music
decisions.reason: Readable names the instruments together as his music.
